summary.one_sentence: CoALA turns language agents into a cognitive-architecture design problem by separating memory modules, internal and external actions, and a looping decision procedure.
summary.thesis: Recent LLM agents share recurring internal mechanisms, but custom terminology hides their common structure; importing cognitive-architecture concepts gives agent builders a reusable vocabulary and blueprint.
summary.why_it_matters: For agent infrastructure, CoALA names the runtime pieces that need explicit interfaces: working state, long-term stores, tool/environment grounding, retrieval, reasoning, learning, and the top-level decision loop.

prior_state: Early language agents often placed an LLM directly in a feedback loop with an external environment.
Newer agents added reasoning, planning, reflection, retrieval, and memory, but papers used inconsistent names for similar mechanisms.
Traditional cognitive architectures had mature notions of working memory, long-term memory, grounding, learning, and decision cycles, but required hand-specified symbolic rules.
problem.key_gap: The paper addresses the lack of a systematic framework for comparing existing language agents and planning new ones at the architectural level.
assumptions: LLMs can be usefully viewed as probabilistic production systems over text.
Text can act as a shared internal representation across memory, reasoning, and grounding procedures.
Conceptual decomposition is useful even when the paper does not provide a new empirical benchmark.

concepts.name: LLM as probabilistic production system
concepts.definition: A language model defines a distribution over text completions or rewrites, making each model call analogous to selecting a production under a probabilistic controller.

concepts.name: CoALA memory hierarchy
concepts.definition: The agent state is organized into working memory plus long-term episodic, semantic, and procedural memories.

concepts.name: Internal and external actions
concepts.definition: External actions ground the agent in environments; internal actions operate on memory through retrieval, reasoning, and learning.

concepts.name: Decision cycle
concepts.definition: The top-level agent program repeatedly uses reasoning and retrieval to plan, then executes a selected grounding or learning action before looping.

method.core_idea: Map language agents onto a cognitive architecture: keep active state in working memory, persist experience and knowledge in long-term memories, expose grounding/retrieval/reasoning/learning as actions, and run a repeated decision cycle that plans before executing environment or memory-changing actions.
action_grammar: Grounding action: external interaction such as robot control, web navigation, API use, or communication.
Retrieval action: read from long-term memory into working memory.
Reasoning action: use the LLM to update working memory with inferred facts, plans, critiques, or candidate actions.
Learning action: write experience, knowledge, code, prompts, or parameters into long-term memory.
steps: Frame LLM calls and prompt chains as production-like operations over text.
Import cognitive-architecture concepts to define memory modules and action types.
Classify recent agents by their long-term memory, external grounding, internal actions, and decision-making procedure.
Use the classification to identify reusable abstractions and underexplored design directions.

claims.statement: CoALA organizes language agents around three architectural dimensions: information storage, action space, and decision-making procedure.
claims.scope: Framework definition in the introduction and Section 4.
caveats: This is a conceptual organization, not an experimentally validated optimal architecture.

claims.statement: The framework separates working memory from long-term episodic, semantic, and procedural memory.
caveats: The paper mainly discusses text-centric memories and leaves non-text modalities as allowed but less developed.

claims.statement: CoALA divides agent actions into external grounding actions and internal retrieval, reasoning, and learning actions.
claims.scope: Action-space definition in Section 4 and Figure 5.
caveats: The boundary between reasoning and learning can blur in implementations that both generate and persist new procedures.

claims.statement: The top-level agent controller is modeled as a repeated decision cycle with planning and execution stages.
claims.scope: Decision-making procedure in Sections 4.6 and Figure 4B.
caveats: The paper describes the control loop abstractly; concrete schedulers, retry semantics, and failure handling remain implementation choices.

claims.statement: CoALA can express a range of existing agents, including SayCan, ReAct, Voyager, Generative Agents, and Tree of Thoughts, by comparing their memory, grounding, internal actions, and decision-making.
caveats: The table is a retrospective classification; it does not prove that the classification improves those agents' performance.

claims.statement: The paper argues for modular, reusable language-agent abstractions such as Memory, Action, and Agent classes to reduce technical debt and improve compatibility.
caveats: The paper gives design direction, not a production-ready library or compatibility standard.

evidence.result: The paper states that CoALA organizes agents by information storage, action space, and decision-making procedure, then develops those concepts in Section 4.

CoALA defines short-term working memory and long-term episodic, semantic, and procedural memories. Working memory persists active state across LLM calls and connects LLM prompts, long-term memory, and grounding interfaces.
The paper separates external grounding actions from internal memory actions, and decomposes internal actions into retrieval, reasoning, and learning.
The decision procedure repeatedly uses reasoning and retrieval to propose, evaluate, and select alternatives during planning, then executes a grounding or learning action and loops after observation.

Table 2 casts SayCan, ReAct, Voyager, Generative Agents, and Tree of Thoughts into the CoALA dimensions, showing differences in long-term memory, external grounding, internal actions, and decision-making.

The paper recommends systematic modular design, argues for standardized abstractions analogous to MDP/Gym concepts in reinforcement learning, and suggests company-wide agent libraries for reuse and testing.

agent_infra_takeaways: Treat agent memory as typed runtime state, not only prompt text: working, episodic, semantic, and procedural stores have different persistence and mutation semantics.
Separate internal actions from external side effects. Retrieval, reasoning, and learning should be inspectable runtime operations before a grounding action touches the world.
The decision loop is the agent's main procedure, so production runtimes need explicit scheduling, observation capture, action parsing, and replay boundaries.
Procedural memory is broader than model weights: prompts, parsers, code skills, retrieval procedures, and learning policies can all become mutable agent state.
The framework is useful as a schema for reviews because it forces each paper to say which memory, action, and decision components it actually changes.
caveats: CoALA is primarily a conceptual framework and survey, not a new empirical agent with benchmark results.
The framework does not by itself solve safety, permissions, persistence, or exactly-once execution for side-effecting agents.
The paper's categories are intentionally broad, so implementations still need concrete interface contracts and failure handling.
Autonomous updates to source code, retrieval, learning, or decision-making are flagged as risky and underexplored.
The paper assumes text is the dominant internal representation, while multimodal and embodied settings may require richer state.

related_work.title: Soar
related_work.note: Traditional cognitive architecture used to explain working memory, long-term memory, productions, and decision cycles.

related_work.title: ReAct
related_work.note: CoALA classifies ReAct as using internal reasoning plus external grounding but lacking long-term semantic or episodic memory.

related_work.title: Voyager
related_work.note: Used as an example of procedural memory and learning by adding code-based grounding skills.

related_work.title: Generative Agents
related_work.note: Used as an example of episodic and semantic memory with reflection over experiences.

poc.note: No PoC yet - contributions welcome. A useful local PoC would implement a tiny CoALA runtime skeleton with typed working, episodic, semantic, and procedural stores plus logged internal/external actions.
